speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF INCARCERATION ON PRISONERS OF WAR IN EUROPE DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 41(2) I wish at this time to table in both official languages a report of a study on Canadians who were prisoners of war in Europe during World War II. I hope it will be possible in the near future to refer this report to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs for consideration.
Hon. members may recall that in June, 1972, the standing committee recommended that the government should arrange to have a study made to identify any physiological and psychological long-terms effects which incarceration might have had on these veterans. The government accepted this recommendation, and on January 31 of last year I announced that the study was being undertaken by Dr. J. Douglas Hermann of Ottawa. This work has now been completed. The author of the report not only offered his conclusions on the medical effects of imprisonment but also volunteered a number of recommendations. On the whole, the government considers that these recommendations should not be accepted, but is withholding its final decision until its receives the report of the standing committee.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF INCARCERATION ON PRISONERS OF WAR IN EUROPE DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for sending me a copy of the Hermann report following a study on Canadians who were prisoners of war in Europe. While it is quite complex and will require extensive deliberation by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, we welcome it and commend Dr. Hermann for producing the facts which will
enlighten those who are concerned with the effect on the lives of Canadian veterans who suffered health defects as a result of treatment in prisoner of war camps.
I am disappointed, though, that the minister indicated in his statement that the government considers these recommendations should not be accepted but is withholding its final decision until it receives the report of the standing committee. This is the kind of promise that is not a promise. I hope that in the standing committee we can change the government's mind in view of the recommendations we will bring before parliament as a result of our deliberations.
It is significant, Mr. Speaker, that after so many years we are only finally determining, with facts, that the Dieppe prisoners of war have experienced a higher mortality rate from cardiovascular disease and other heart diseases than others, and identifying the psychological and physiological long-term effects. This emphasizes, to me, our continued responsibility toward our war veterans as long as they live.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF INCARCERATION ON PRISONERS OF WAR IN EUROPE DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF INCARCERATION ON PRISONERS OF WAR IN EUROPE DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
It is our responsibility on a continuing basis because most prisoners of war have aged prematurely and will continue to have a shorter life span than those who were lucky enough to return unharmed or who were lucky enough to remain at home. The details of the group study points out the high percentage of survivors who were forced to resort to pensions, comparative low standards of earnings and low standards of homes, with a resulting number of premature deaths.
Finally, we have a responsibility for those who returned maimed and disabled and continue to struggle to maintain a normal, reasonable standard of existence. I hope that this report will be referred to the standing committee as soon as possible so that we in parliament can continue to recommend legislation in order to fulfil our commitments to the veterans of Canada.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF INCARCERATION ON PRISONERS OF WAR IN EUROPE DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) in commending Dr. Hermann on a thorough study and an excellent report on Canadians who were prisoners of war in Europe during World War II. The study deals in particular with those who were prisoners of war following the Dieppe engagement but it also covers other prisoners of war in Europe.
However, sir, like my colleague from Newfoundland, I am deeply disappointed that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), even before most members have seen the report, has announced that the government considers that these recommendations should not be accepted.
November 18, 1974

Indian Affairs
For the past two years, veterans who were prisoners of war in Europe have dared to hope that because a study of their case was being made, recommendations meeting their needs would come forth and that the government and parliament would act on those recommendations.
The recommendations are very few. In the main, it is recommended that there be appropriate compensation on a continuing basis over and above all disability pensions already awarded to Dieppe prisoners of war. There is a recommendation that appropriate compensation also be granted to prisoners of war in other parts of Europe. The third and very important recommendation-it reminds me of one that was in the Woods report-calls for widows whose husbands were on less than 48 per cent pension at the time of death to be awarded pensions prorated, rather than nothing at all as is the present case. The other recommendation has to do with continued study.
It seems to me that these are excellent and appropriate recommendations. I believe they will commend themselves to members on all sides of the House. I believe they will commend themselves to veterans and veterans' organizations and that the Canadian public would want these recommendations to be accepted, and I regret that the minister has said no right off the bat. I trust that when this matter is referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, the whips will be off, and that the committee will be free to make its own recommendations back to parliament on what is to be done as a result of this report. If this is the case, I believe the recommendation will be that the Hermann report be implemented.

Once again, I am very happy to join my colleagues in working, in committee, on a bill that will allow us to alleviate the hardships of those prisoners.

subsubtopic: RESTRICTIONS OF OPERATIONAL ROLES OF FORCES- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I should like to ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. This is the first such motion I have ever moved. I have an opinion about how dubious this procedure is from time to time. However, because of the subject matter I am presenting the motion at this time. I am asking for unanimous consent to move this motion of urgent and pressing necessity in \ iew of the pathetic statement made to this House by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) on November 13, and his statement on Friday last, that surveillance of our coasts was taking place. Since sovereignty of our shores is supposed to be the top priority of our forces and present restrictions in the operations of Maritime Command have reduced our surveillance in the north to one flight every six months, next to no effective coastal patrol and no joint exercises whatsoever with our NATO allies, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall):
That the Minister of National Defence forthwith make a statement outlining what we are not doing now, which we were doing before present financial restrictions affected defence operations, and what plans the minister has for the future, so that some purpose and commitment can replace the present mood of despair and depression which presently permeates our forces.

FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO INSTITUTE BARILOCHE IN ARGENTINA
speechtext:
1.	Did the International Development Research Centre provide financial assistance to the Institute Bariloche in Argentina and, if so, what were the terms, conditions and amount of that financial assistance?

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO INSTITUTE BARILOCHE IN ARGENTINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the question is as follows:
1.	The International Development Research Centre made a grant of $81,000 in July, 1972 to the Fundacion Bariloche in Buenos Aires, to help a team of Latin American scientists design a mathematical world model as an alternative to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology model that was popularized in the book "The Limits of Growth". A supplemental grant of $31,500 was made in November 1973 to allow the group to complete their project and to pay, among other items, the cost of extra computer time. The funds were paid in three instalments, and a condition of the grant is the requirement that the Fundacion make a financial reporting of the expenditures incurred during each instalment period.
2.	A first progress report of the early results of the group's work was presented at a Club of Rome meeting in Tokyo in December, 1973. The work was further elaborated during 1974, and a more complete presentation made in Vienna in September, 1974. A draft report, about 80 pages long, summarizing the work and conclusions of the Bariloche group is now being revised by its Latin American authors in the light of comments from the Vienna meeting and elsewhere. The International Development Research Centre hopes to publish this document as soon as possible after its revision and, if so, it will certainly be available to members of parliament.

speechtext:
that Bill C-10, to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the cash advance legislation has been an important part of the available means for farmers to obtain cash in the prairies apart from actual delivery opportunities. At the time the legislation was first introduced there were long delays in the delivering of the farmer's crop to the Canadian Wheat Board. We were in a situation for a number of years where the whole of the farmer's crop could not be delivered during the course of the crop year. The situation has changed considerably and in that regard we have been going through a period of years, including this year, when quotas have opened rather rapidly and indeed to very high levels during the course of the crop year. At this point, for instance, although we are only several months into the crop year there is not only a significant quota on all grades of wheat but the quota for the top grade is in fact open, so that farmers have a tremendous delivery opportunity.
Notwithstanding this, the cash advance legislation should not be neglected, and in our view should be kept in tune with the possible needs for important cash early in the season in advance of delivery opportunities. Indeed, it should be noted by the House that the commitment to increase the maximum in the cash advance legislation from $6,000 to $15,000 was part of the over-all review of our feed grain policy and the introduction of the opportunity for farmers to deliver their feed grains and wheat,

November 18, 1974
Grain
oats and barley to the domestic market without delivering them to the Canadian Wheat Board. At that point we wanted to emphasize that while the farmer should have that opportunity-the choice to deliver domestically outside of the board or, particularly for export purposes, to the board-we wanted him to make a judgment on the basis of the merits of the two opportunities and not on the basis of cash pressure in the event he wanted to deliver to the Canadian Wheat Board.
In the case of deliveries to the board, the farmer receives an initial price for his wheat which does not represent its total value. In the case of the open market, he normally receives the full value that he would receive for the grain and he must compare an immediate, full cash price with another price which may well be greater but which will be partly cash and partly a payment to be made in due course when the various circumstances which affect the market have had their play and the Wheat Board is able to determine the total balance of the pool and make a distribution to the farmers. It may be noted that on occasion the initial price and the total receipts of farmers have differed fairly widely, although ordinarily final payments have been fairly modest. Just today I indicated in a notice to the House that initial prices were being increased effective Monday, November 25, to recognize the current buoyant circumstances of prices for wheat, oats and barley. We are increasing the levels of these initial prices to those in effect in the last crop year from March 1 until July 31.
In the case of No. 1 CW, and in the case of barley, we are raising the prices specifically to those levels. In the case of oats, we are introducing a 10 cent increase in the initial price, which will make it 10 cents higher than was the case in the latter part of the last crop year, in recognition of market conditions in regard to oats. I should emphasize, in passing, that the prices announced today are for the basic grades only. The actual prices for the other grades, the differential for Durum, the differential for grades in tough and damp condition, and all the differentials for other grades except these base grades will be announced within the week as determined on the recommendation of the Canadian Wheat Board, having regard to all the circumstances that affect these various grades and conditions. They may well vary in degree in the increase in those initial prices from the increase in the base grades that have been announced.
This bill is relevant to the feed grain policy because it will assist the farmer by providing cash advances, thus allowing him to receive a portion of the cash he will be entitled to when he delivers his grain later to the Canadian Wheat Board and to receive the cash advance without at that point having a quota to deliver on. To the extent that need for cash would otherwise be a pressure upon him to deliver to the open market, whether his judgment leads him there or not, that pressure is removed by these cash advances. It was with this in view that we thought the level of the advances should be raised in terms of the maximum per producer. When the program was introduced, the maximum was $3,000 for producers. Several years later it was doubled to $6,000, and now we propose to increase it to $15,000.
These are simply advances on the amount of money that farmers would otherwise receive upon delivery of their

grain, but they are made as though they are payments in advance and for that reason they are, generally speaking, interest-free. The cash, therefore, is in the hands of the farmer as though he had a delivery opportunity early in the season, rather than later. Cash advances will always be less useful or necessary, I suppose, when the farmer's cash receipts are higher and therefore he has cash available and is in a better position to meet his needs. The current cash position in the grain producing area is extremely favourable. Hon. members will have recently noticed figures for the whole of Canada which show that farmers' cash receipts are up to more than 43 per cent in the first nine-month period of 1974.
They will have noticed, too, that in the province by province analysis the greatest increases have taken place in the prairie provinces. Saskatchewan leads the way with cash receipts which have moved to $1.93 billion for the nine-month period, from $1.02 billion for the corresponding period a year earlier. That is an increase of approximately 90 per cent for Saskatchewan, over what I believe was itself a record. If one were to take grain figures alone, this situation would be further emphasized. Indeed, it is demonstrated by the way in which the Saskatchewan- and, to a lesser degree, Alberta and Manitoba-figures of cash receipts for farmers perform during the same period. Farmers may, nonetheless, require cash earlier in the delivery year because of the necessity to obtain supplies, such as fertilizer, for the fall and the following season. Even in such a buoyant year, cash advances may be an element in the over-all farm picture. This increase is therefore proceeded with at this time notwithstanding the buoyant position.
On at least one occasion in the past, cash advances were used as a form of stabilization. Several years ago, when delivery opportunities fell to their lowest ebb, cash advances were allowed to exceed the actual amounts that could be recovered on them. Our decision to proceed with a logical and full-scale stabilization program for grains in the prairie region means that this will no longer be necessary. The increase is desirable, however, for other reasons, particularly to allow the farmer to have his cash in advance of delivery opportunity and therefore to balance the fact that this cash is available to him in full in the open market.
The bill increases the maximum available for an individual farmer from $6,000 to $15,000. It also permits recognition of the fact that in certain circumstances more than one person per permit is engaged in full-time farming. The new limit of $15,000 will, therefore, be multiplied by two or by three, as the case may be, where there are two or more real farmers represented by the permit book.
Cash advances have had an extraordinarily good record of repayment by farmers who have benefited from them. In many past years, 99.99 per cent of cash advances were repaid in due course by farmers in the prairie region. This is an outstanding record and I know it will not surprise those hon. members who are conscious of the attitude of the farmers in question and know their willingness to co-operate in plans which they can see are for their benefit.

This legislation was proposed in the last part of the previous session of parliament before dissolution. At that time it would have been possible to introduce the higher maximum for the current crop year. The dissolution of parliament and the ensuing election rendered that impossible, but we hope the legislation will be passed now and will be in operation for the next crop year. I think it is an important part of our over-all endeavour to protect the prairie farmer and to give him a total system of cash and returns to meet his needs, not only in terms of the amount of that remuneration but in terms of the time period in which he will receive it.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore commend Bill C-10 to the House and invite hon. members to refer it to the Standing Committee on Agriculture with dispatch for examination in detail. I think this has been recognized on all sides of the House as an extremely useful program for prairie farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on Bill C-10, I must say that I was interested to hear the minister explain the reason for the bill. It should first be pointed out that cash advance legislation was introduced by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) some 15 or 16 years ago. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) suggests it was 17 years ago, and I believe that is correct. It is interesting to note that the Liberal Party has had a change of heart in the interim period.
At the time the legislation was introduced they said this could not be done, they would not do it, and if it was ever done it would cost the companies huge sums of money, the farmers would not pay it back, and so on. They violently opposed this legislation at first. Now they are enlarging it and the minister gave two reasons for this. I will paraphrase what he said, Mr. Speaker. First of all the minister said that cash advance legislation must be updated. Well, it must keep up with inflation. The cost of production has been going up, and I am pleased to see the government recognizes that. By increasing the cash advance limit from $6,000 to $15,000, the government acknowledges that inflation plays a part.
The minister said that the other purpose of this legislation was the cash pressure on the farmer to sell his grain on the open market. I have come to the conclusion that this is the main reason the legislation is before the House today. Last year the government introduced a feed grains policy which allows the farmer to sell grain to either the Canadian Wheat Board or to the elevator companies. That grain is kept on the open market; it is bought at whatever the going price is and sold at the going price. The minister says this legislation is necessary in order to avert the cash pressure on the farmer to sell on the open market. It is my understanding that grain companies are to keep 10 per cent of their storage capacity open for feed grains on the open market.
The minister also spoke about the increase in the initial price. Members on this side of the House have long advocated the setting of the initial price based on a formula related to the expected price. I have used the figures of 75 per cent to 80 per cent. In other words, the initial price should be 75 per cent of the final price. The minister has played around with the figures for the beginning of
Grain
this crop year, but in fact at the end of the 1972-73 crop year the initial price received was $3.75 per bushel of wheat, basis Fort William; $2.25 per bushel of barley, basis Fort William; and $1.10 per bushel of oats, basis Fort William. The announcement made by the minister today merely reinstates the initial price for wheat and barley and adds ten cents per bushel to the price of oats.
The minister has not followed any formula in setting initial prices, and this bill does not guide farmers. The original intent of the cash advance legislation was to provide cash to farmers who had about one billion bushels stored on the farm. The farmer who operated under the acreage or permit book system could go to the elevator company and receive a cash advance of up to $3,000. Subsequently, the amount was raised to $6,000 but the basic principle of the legislation was not changed. The cash advance program eased the pressure on the farmer who was short of cash. Under this bill, the government wishes to encourage farmers to sell through the Wheat Board and not on the open market. The government is saying, "We do not want you to sell on the open market. Sell through the Wheat Board and we will give you a cash advance."
Cash advance legislation was introduced 17 years ago for justifiable reasons. It is to be reinstated on the statute books, but this time it is designed to offset the weak feed grains policy which the minister introduced about one year ago. So let's not kid the troops. This is not the same old cash advance legislation, and the minister knows it. The amount of grain in storage on farms at the end of the 1973 crop year does not compare with the amount in storage 17 years ago. Today, farmers are not worried if they can sell grain or get cash for it. The minister has told the House about the number of farmers who deferred collecting money due to them from grain sales made this fall. He did not tell us how much money the Wheat Board is holding back in deferred payments. I suggest that the board is holding back about $500 million in deferred payments which farmers could collect if they wanted to. But the minister did not mention that. The announcement made today reads:
With the higher initial payments, Mr. Lang also announced that an adjustment payment will be made to all those producers who have already delivered wheat, barley and oats to the Canadian Wheat Board since the beginning of the current crop year on August 1, 1974-

The minister said he would not make final payments on 1973-74 pool accounts before January 1. Two years ago, when the minister found it politically expedient to do the opposite, he did so. At one time, final payments were never made before January or February. In the year of the October 30 election the minister said that the pool accounting system could be speeded up and payments made on August 1, before the end of the crop year. Now the minister has changed his mind and has said no final payment will be made on the 1973-74 pool account until January next because farmers are worried about income tax; that is, the payment on grain already delivered will not be made until January.

Even those who know absolutely nothing about farming should realize that if the final payment on the 1973-74 crop year is not made until the 1974-75 crop year, it may look as if initial payments have been increased. Actually, all that will have happened is that certain payments have been deferred; farmers will receive deferred payments for crops they have sold. Quite conceivably, such deferred payments could amount to between $400 million and $500 million next year. So one can see what happens when farmers do not pick up all their money. The question is, why is the minister pretending that this new legislation merely updates the former cash advance legislation, when he knows that we need to correct the situation created by his feed grain policy? I think the minister is worried about that policy. I ask the minister to consider the fact that the companies are buying feed grains at an alarming rate on the open market and this is undermining the government's policy of encouraging farmers to hold their grain and sell it through the Wheat Board in return for the privilege of cash advances.
When he introduced the legislation this afternoon the minister did not say if the amount per bushel advanced is to be increased, or how cash advances are to be paid back. When the minister introduced his first proposal covering cash advances, I prophesied that farmers would draw money out more quickly than they could pay it back. I said that the fund would not work. A year of so later the minister adjusted the program. I gather that under the present program there is to be no change in how much a farmer may have advanced to him. There is to be no change in the amount a farmer can receive as an advance and there is no change in the manner in which it is to be paid back. Therefore, we must examine the concept of the policy the minister is introducing.
For many years, if a family farm corporation worked under one permit book it was entitled to a cash advance as a single entity. Now, each member of the corporation, if it is a partnership or co-op, can borrow up to $15,000. This means that two shareholders, or farmers, can receive up to $30,000 in cash advances. Three or more shareholders, or partners, can receive up to $45,000. Clearly, a corresponding amount of grain must be sold. Thus, the minister has changed the permit book system substantially and the practice followed over the years is to be changed. I suggest that the minister has brought forward this legislation as a result of faults which have developed in his feed grains policy.
We have experienced many difficulties in grain production and in agriculture and the minister has done little to help. He made a great speech to the Grains Council a month ago suggesting that the Crowsnest pass rates should be done away with. Doing this, he said, would facilitate the movement of feed grain at a cheaper rate. How he arrives at that conclusion would be difficult to explain. In any case, it is now well established that farmers are not delivering their grain to the Wheat Board. They are withholding it for a variety of reasons: one has to do with income tax; and another is that they want to determine what they are likely to get for it on the open market as feed.
Recently a number of farmers asked me how best they could sell their barley, whether to sell it on the open market or through the Wheat Board. They wanted to know where they would get the best return. In announcing today that the initial price is to be increased, the minister did not tell us by how much. We understand that demurrage charges with respect to the crop year 1973-74 are to be carried over the crop year 1974-75. This may well affect the final payment for that crop year.
Some months ago there was a great deal of discussion about hopper cars and the Wheat Board suggested that producers would be in the business of buying and building hopper cars. The question that occurs to me is this: would the cost be charged against the Wheat Board account but not against grain moving under the feed grains policy? Some months ago, prior to an election, I think, the minister went to great lengths to suggest that the government would pay for repairing box cars. Are we to learn that this money will come out of the Wheat Board account and not out of receipts from grain sold on the open market for feed in Canada?
I believe it may well come out of the Wheat Board capital account. Why? Some months ago I asked the minister a question in this House about the demurrage charges incurred at Vancouver because grain was not being loaded. It was not being loaded through any fault of the farmer or of the grain companies; it was the fault of the government-the government had intervened to bring about a situation which lasted for some three months. The minister replied unequivocally that demurrage charges would come out of the Wheat Board account. I said at the time that this would mean more than $10 million coming out of that account because of the failure of the government to act with regard to the grain handlers strike. If the minister can tell us that the demurrage charges should come out of the Wheat Board account, why should he not tell us also that the money for the repair of boxcars would come from that account; that is, if one follows the minister's logic? I cannot do so: it is very difficult because the minister works in mysterious ways.

speechtext: The hon. member knows perfectly well that the treasury is paying for these repairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
The minister wants farmers to believe that this cash advance legislation is needed for the same purpose as similar legislation 17 years ago. He told us that some kind of subsidy would be devised in connection with ending the Crowsnest pass rates. Farmers were told, in effect, "Don't despair. Instead of giving money to the railroads, we will give it directly to you." Of course, that was before the election. I often think the farmer may get something periodically, two months or so before an election. On one occasion, before the election which was held on October 30, 1972, the minister was a little late with the payment; he announced it 15 days before the election. Farmers resented that open bribery and rejected the minister on that occasion.
However, the minister moves in mysterious ways and he wants to convince us that this legislation is necessary for the same reason as the cash advances of 17 years ago. It is not. Why, then, is he bringing this measure forward? The

November 18, 1974

answer is that he wants it to offset a weakness in his feed grain policy: he is afraid that too much will be sold on the open market rather than through the Wheat Board. Anybody who has grown grain on the prairies realizes the strength of the Wheat Board. A number of people find fault with the board. It has not always worked well, but by and large most farmers support it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: As long as it is left alone.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) says, "As long as the government will let it alone." I recall a speech in which I pointed out that the minister had intervened in the affairs of the board more often than any of his predecessors. I listed all the hon. gentleman's Liberal predecessors: he had tinkered more and caused more concern than all of them put together. Yet at times he does not tinker enough. We saw a railway strike last something like 60 days. The chairman of the Wheat Board was almost in despair over loss of shipments. Then we saw the grain handlers' strike prolonged because of the minister's intervention and the intervention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). We saw that strike go on for two or three months longer than it should have.
Even after the railway strike, terminal workers in some parts of the CN system took part in what is commonly called a slow-wheel movement, at the port of Vancouver. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool contacted the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to ask for assistance in ending that slow-wheel movement which lasted nearly a year-from February, 1973, almost to February, 1974. The president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool says the sale of 16 million bushels was just purely because of that situation.
The minister now comes forward with a small piece of legislation that will have no real effect on the financial and economic climate on the prairies. The last crop year was a relatively good year for grain sales and grain marketings and farmers borrowed $20 million under the cash advance legislation. In 1969, some $272 million was borrowed under the same legislation; but this was the year of operation LIFT, and that and a number of other circumstances made farmers short of cash at a time when there was plenty of grain still in the bins. Each year from 1969 until today the farmers have paid back more than they have borrowed and now net borrowings are down to a low figure.
I suggest the minister would be unable to make any member of the House believe that this cash advance legislation is any cure-all for the difficult marketing situation that may arise this fall, especially with grain that is unsuitable as milling grain. This bill will offer no particular assistance in this regard. Perhaps the minister is attempting to build up for some large, wealthy corporate undertaking cash advances interest-free. For example, $45,000 borrowed at today's interest rates would mean $4,500 in interest alone. This is the largest amount that any corporation, company, partnership, or father-son operation can borrow under this legislation, provided they have the necessary grain. So I would not be at all surprised to see some grain farmers in parts of Saskatchewan borrowing
Grain
$45,000 from the elevator companies, putting the money in the bank and collecting the interest on it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: What an awful thing to say!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member suggests that that is an awful thing to say. I readily admit that the truth sometimes hurts. The point I am making is that if the minister wants to enable the farmers to set aside money which they can reinvest at the opportune time-in other words, to set aside a fund to smooth over some of the ups and downs in their operation-then he should do so by greatly changing the system, by introducing something similar to what I might call a registered retirement Savings plan, in which farmers can build up a nest-egg to help them over difficult periods. This kind of system would be helpful to the agricultural industry, particularly the livestock breeders.
The members of the agriculture committee will have to take a very close look at this bill and the whole question of cash pressure exerted on farmers today due to the change in feed grains policy. The committee must determine whether this cash pressure is encouraging farmers to sell grain on the open market which normally would have gone to the Canadian Wheat Board. If that in fact is the case, surely we require legislation that more directly deals with this question, rather than using legislation that is already on the statue books.
I would be remiss if I did not bring another matter to the attention of the minister. When he introduced the new feed grains policy he also assured the livestock industry that their cost of transportation would be comparable to the cost of transporting grain via the railroads to eastern Canada. If the minister regards this bill as being part and parcel of his feed grains policy, then we on this side of the House will be waiting anxiously for the other part of his feed grains policy. I wonder why the minister has not introduced that part this year, at a time when the price of Stocker cattle in western Canada is so low. Why has he not lived up to the obligation he undertook?
For example, he could have increased the price of calves a cent or two per pound, which would have meant a great deal, particularly at a time when farmers have been asking the federal government to assist the cattle industry, whether in the Peace River area, in northern or southern Saskatchewan, Manitoba or, for that matter, in the Cariboo in British Columbia. The cattle industry has been looking to the federal government for some over-all recognition that the price of feeder cattle today is not what it should be, and they are also looking for freight rates comparable to the rate for moving feed grains.
Having said that, I will watch with interest the progress of this legislation, since I think its purpose has strayed a long way from its original purpose 17 years ago. One wonders whether the minister is doing all he can to live up to his feed grains policy, and whether his feed grains policy will do all he and many others thought it would do when it was announced in the first part of August.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no question that all members of the House will support this legislation in principle. This has been the case since it was first brought before parliament in 1957, after many years of requests for the legislation from farm

November 18, 1974
Grain
organizations, certainly from my own party and, I believe, from the party to my right during the late 1940s and 1950. Since there is no argument about the principle of the legislation, there is no need for the debate to go on at any length; but there are some questions that I hope the minister and his colleagues will consider and do something about when the bill goes to the committee on agriculture.
I have a few points to make and I pass them to the minister for consideration; he may already be aware of them. I understand there is concern among the grain companies over the administration of the cash advance legislation. They are somewhat anxiously waiting to see what agreement the Wheat Board will be submitting to them, since the agreement requires the grain companies, and subsequently the grain elevator agents, to be liable for the loss of any cash advances. I readily agree with the minister that there has been little or no problem since the legislation was first introduced. In fact, if the government were as reliable as the farmers in respect of cash advances, we would be much better off. I would remind the minister that the elevator agent can only take the word of the farmer regarding how much grain the farmer has, when issuing a cash advance. It is not practical or feasible for the elevator agent to go around inspecting every farmyard and granary to see whether farmers have the grain for delivery in order to repay cash advances.
The other point I want to make, on behalf of the elevator agents, is that while they have a liability in respect of the recovery of cash advances, they receive no compensation for handling what is probably half the administration involved in the cash advance legislation. These agents do a great deal of paperwork. This relieves the government and the Canadian Wheat Board from at least this administrative aspect, yet the elevator agent receives no compensation. It should be incumbent upon the government to see that when agreement in respect of the administration of this legislation is arrived at between the grain companies and the Canadian Wheat Board, some measure of compensation is made available to the elevator agents who administer the legislation and are faced with some liability under it.
Regarding the new limits in the legislation, I should like to ask the minister whether he would consider some change in respect of co-operative farms which may have anywhere from 5 to 20 members, in view of the fact that the $45,000 maximum is often insufficient. I have already spoken to a member of the Matador co-op farm, of which I believe there are presently 19 members, who said that in periods when there are many deliveries the $45,000 cash advance maximum is entirely insufficient. I appreciate that this does not involve a large number of farmers, but the minister and 1 know there are a number of co-operative farms with from three to a dozen or more members, and the maximum cash advance will not be very useful to them. I hope he will consider making exceptions in the case of co-operative farms with a large number of members, thereby providing higher maximum cash advances.
I was pleased to hear the minister announce today an increase in initial prices, as this has been demanded by members on this side, as well as farmers and farm organi-

zations, for many months. There is no question in my mind that the low initial payments being made were nothing more than coercion on the farmer to get him to deliver grain on the open market. As long as the initial prices were below open market prices and the farmer needed cash to meet his harvest expenses, and so on, he had to sell his grain on the open market and most of the time he was not inclined to do so. I hope the new initial price structure the minister has announced will bring the price into line with the open market price.
Having regard to the argument that has been going on between the minister and myself and between the minister and farmers and farm organizations, let me say that it will continue. The whole policy in respect of feed grains is something the farmers thought they got rid of once and for all after the world war. When the minister brought in this feed grains program he told the farmers it was a good program and said he was fully in support of the Canadian Wheat Board and orderly marketing. Although he said the feed grains program was good, he hoped farmers would not deliver grain on the open market but would sell it to the Canadian Wheat Board. For many months the initial price was so low that many farmers had no real choice but to sell on the open market.
I hope that this increase in the initial price will do a great deal to encourage farmers not to deliver grain on the open market. I suppose in this one area the minister and I agree, in that we both hope his feed grain policy will collapse, with no deliveries being made on the open market. This whole policy can do nothing but cause deterioration in orderly marketing and the effectiveness of the Canadian Wheat Board. It seems there was no reason for bringing in that policy other than to detract from the principle of orderly marketing. The farmers did not ask for this feed grains policy, and I am sure neither the grain companies nor the wheat pools asked for it. Farmers' organizations and others still do not know why the minister was moved to bring in this policy or why he felt it was necessary. As far as I am concerned, there was only one reason for it; that was, to try to restore some degree of strength in the Winnipeg commodity exchange to the benefit of speculators and others who like to make a living off the backs of others without doing very much themselves.
The announced increase in initial payments will be welcomed by the farmers and the grain companies. In fact, the minister's announcement today in this regard effectively cut my speech in half, because I intended to say a lot more but now find it unnecessary. In any event, I should like to make a couple of other points on the issue raised by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). For some time now, successive governments in Canada have played off grain growers against livestock growers, and vice-versa. For years the livestock growers had things pretty good and the grain growers had things pretty bad. Now, with higher grain prices, the situation is reversed, with the result that grain growers are better off and cattle prices are in a mess. These two Canadian groups are almost at each other's throats because of the inadequacy of national policies in this area.
Here again I should like to put forward the suggestion that the two-price system which applies to feed grains is
November 18, 1974

just as logical in respect of grain for human consumption. There is no reason why the Wheat Board's world asking price cannot be put in place, with a second price being in place for domestic consumption whether it be for human consumption or livestock feeding. That price should have some relation to the farmer's cost of production, and the world price would be of benefit to the producer. This would mean that the price of feed grain would be such as to take into consideration the needs of the livestock industry. I hope the minister and his colleagues will move in this direction.
Such a system with two prices would work a disadvantage to the private grain operators and speculators on the Winnipeg commodity exchange, but I am hopeful that the minister and this government are prepared to move in this direction. I can assure the minister that my colleagues and I will continue to promote this idea. Such legislation is urgently required by farmers in times of high grain deliveries. It would offset the situation which often occurs when we have a winter such as the last one. I might add that the situation is aggravated by the fact that the railroad companies have done nothing to improve the standard of hundreds of miles of their trackage: this will mean that many farmers in a number of areas will not receive rail service and will not be able to deliver their grain.
These advances will be welcomed and will be used particularly by the growers located on what the minister and his experts call low-density lines. They are low-density because the railways do not run trains over them. This is another way of coercing farmers to deliver grain over longer distances to secondary or main line points. The farmers must either do this, at higher cost, or take advantage of the cash advances.
This is another reason I hope farmers will take advantage of the cash advances when they find themselves in this kind of situation and will refuse to deliver grain over longer distances to suit the policies of the government regarding branch line abandonment, designed for the convenience of the railways and the grain companies rather than for the convenience of the farmers and the public.
As I have said, we support this legislation in principle. I hope the minister will consider the two points I have made. The first is that there should be some measure of compensation for the elevator agents, who have to do most of the administering of the program and receive nothing in return, while being subject to some liability under it. Second, I hope the minister will consider an exception to the legislation in respect of the $45,000 maximum in the case of co-operative farms with more than three members, so they may have use of cash advances in proportion to the use that may be made by one, two or three farmers. I am pleased to say that we will support the legislation, and hope it will pass quickly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill C-10. First of all I would like to congratualte the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) for the help extended to western grain producers. I listened earlier to the Tory spokesman who said that farmers had been waiting for
Grain
this bill for a long time. A few moments ago the NDP spokesman asked the minister who had prompted him to introduce this bill because he said it seemed co-ops had not asked for this bill. We have here one of the minor inconsistencies that may crop up in this House.
That bill was introduced by the Tories nearly 17 years ago. We note ironically that the Liberals of that time had voted against that bill. Today, they are the ones who want to strengthen it, recognizing the need for such a bill after 17 years.
I am quite happy for the western grain producers because the recommendations read as follows, and I quote:
-to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act to increase from six thousand dollars to fifteen thousand dollars the maximum amount that may be paid to a producer as advance payments in respect of grain to be delivered under a permit book, and under the circumstances prescribed, to privide where a producer is a multi-farmer unit of two shareholders for the maximum amount of thirty thousand dollars, and where the producer is a multi-farmer unti of three or more shareholders for the maximum amount of forty-five thousand dollars.
I think it is simply normal. After 17 years it is time to get in line with today's prices, keep pace with the economy, in view of the spiralling increase in grain prices in recent years.
I think it was simple logic. It is not a favour that the minister is presently doing directly to western producers, he is only following a logical line of thought for the purpose of giving more freedom to western farmers. I think it is the only way for western farmers to go on the open market without always being a little bit of a victim of the Canadian Wheat Board, even though the latter has always done a great job in western Canada. I believe that is the option of competition and it gives western producers another ace in the hole so that they can go to the open market without always being faced with a financial problem.
All that is very nice for the West, we are very happy about it and we also would wish-and I have said this several times since I have been sitting here,-to have an association so that we may obtain federal aid. We too would like to have an association responsible to a minister just like today's Canadian Wheat Board. We, in Quebec, would like to have feed grains organization responsible to a minister. So that the three western provinces could at last trade directly, on equal footing, with the eastern provinces.
I think that is the root of the problem and the origin of all those skirmishes going on between Eastern and Western Canada. We never agree. Why? Because there is always some middleman who is interested in provoking these skirmishes and that middleman is the marketing agent. As long as we are not ridden of those marketing agents we will always be faced with problems. Such is the situation in Quebec these days. After so many years, we still must go through marketing agents to get our wheat from the Prairie provinces. There will be justice in the Eastern provinces only when we have a similar agency in the East to bargain directly with the Western provinces. That organization, for example, an eastern Board responsible to a minister. Why not?
The West has a minister who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. To be fair, let us put a minister in

November 18, 1974
Grain
charge of it and get rid of those financial agencies that gobble up the profits of western producers and eastern consumers. That is the problem, Mr. Speaker. As long as we hang on to those agencies, as long as we refuse to grab the bull by the horns and say: The East is going to be responsible for its purchases from the West, and the two groups will negotiate and come to an agreement without the financiers keeping the better part of the pie, the situation will remain the same.
That is the point I particularly wanted to put before the minister, Mr. Speaker. I am happy that bill has been introduced because it gives us the opportunity to discuss a problem that has been denounced in this House for 10 years but that no one wants to deal with. Neither Quebec nor the other eastern provinces dare make a move to discuss things with the western provinces. The Easterners criticize the Westerners, and vice versa. Everyone seems to be wearing dark glasses that keep them from locating the problem.
I therefore urge the minister to reflect on this problem and I point out to the members of the committee that while I agree with that increase other remedies are indicated which might mean prosperity for the eastern provinces and peace between East and West.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to enter this debate on Bill C-10 until the minister aroused me from my lethargy by putting on record the income that farmers in western Canada are earning. If any person has to be straightened out on this issue, it is the minister. First, I would like to say, for the sake of clarification, that the cash advance legislation of 1957-and this holds true in 1974-is not a hand-out by the federal taxpayer to the western farmer. The farmer pays it back. It is a moral acceptance that when a man earns wages during a calendar year, he has the right to some of them in the year in which he earned them and should not have to wait for that income for two or three years, as was the case in the 1950s.
I was the minister who drafted the legislation in the fall of 1957 as a member of the Diefenbaker administration. I well recall the time when advisers to the government said it was impossible to bring in this type of legislation. It had been put forward in the previous administration on two separate occasions, and for the several reasons advanced by the advisers to the government the previous administration had turned it down. That shows us the great power in the early 1950s of the advisers to take over the minds and souls of the Liberal Party. Nothing has changed. I mentioned the year 1957 for another reason, that is, that at that time farmers all across the country were in a desperate position; hunger was growing in the world and we were sitting on our reserves in Canada. Now that the clock has turned full-cycle and the country is becoming aware that we are in another cycle of great food shortages in the world, suddenly this government becomes interested in the world food program.
I go back in my mind to the years 1973 and 1974 and find the record shows that only one member of this House was asking questions about the shortage of food in the world.

Now everyone is on to the thing and I am stepping out as the one member letting all these people carry it forward. But the problem has been there for 25 years and it will be there longer than 25 years. I am glad to see other people taking up the cudgel.
Let me return to what the minister said. When he said that cash receipts over the first nine months of this year were 90 per cent higher than they were last year, he left the impression that he wanted to carry across this country-that western farmers were rolling in dough. I know something about the income of western farmers. The difficulties they have had since the 1930s have been told over and over again in the House. Believe me when I say that the first year the western farmer broke even so that his operating expenses and interest on the money invested equalled his income was 1972. In 1973 in Saskatchewan, when all these high prices were in effect, he not only paid his expenses, paid himself the interest he had never paid himself before, but made the tremendous amount of $2,200 per family for a whole year's work! That is a fact of life. The year 1973 was the best income year in history for the Saskatchewan farmer, who produces 60 per cent of the grain for export, but he made only $2,200 per family.
I had the impression, from listening to the minister, that now that our income is up so much we are rolling in dough. I would like to see most Canadians across this country trying to live on $2,200 a year. The minister did not mention that in the last three years the average expense of operating a western farm had increased at the rate of 20 per cent, plus, a year. We do not have the figures yet and will not have them until next June for the year 1974, but it seems that the expense increase will hit 25 per cent. As a person who comes from one of the prairie provinces, I know that these expenses will go up. While the average expenses of Canadians have gone up 3 per cent a year, the farmer's costs have gone up 7 per cent. Now that the cost for the rest of Canada is going up by 10 per cent and 11 per cent, farm costs are going up by 20 per cent to 25 per cent. All I know is that when prices go down, costs do not go down but keep on going up.
That brings me to the main point I wanted to make to the minister in all seriousness. He and I have fought across the west on this issue for many years. I hold to the belief that the minister followed the wrong policy from 1968 until 1972 when the government sold western grain on the export market at a price below the cost of production. He argues that that was the right course to follow. That is his view; I have mine. I well remember the election campaign of 1972 when I believe I spoke on behalf of all the farmers who knew how much grain they had in their granaries and on behalf of all those who believed in the organized selling of our grain through a marketing agency which sells grain rather than imposes controls and restrictions. I remember very well saying that we had run out of grain. The price should have gone up in the fall of 1971, on the basis of the information before the government. But the minister, during that hot summer of 1972 said, "There is lots of grain". When the election was over and the price was up to $3 or $5, he was very quiet because there was no grain.
The minister has made horrible blunders in his assessment of the international grain market and that cost has
November 18, 1974

been met by the farmer. In all the years 1968, 1969, 1970, 1971 and 1972 the minister and the government kept grain prices down deliberately on the basis that this was competing. The minister said, "We must remain competitive." That is one point. The second point is that the minister and this government brought in a program in 1970 to take the western grain farmers out of wheat. This minister not only told them to get out of growing wheat, and gave them the inducement of $6 an acre to move into other crops or to summer fallow and hold the land idle, but said, "If you do not do what you are told, you will not be allowed to sell on quota and"-by inference-"you will not be allowed to pay back your cash advances." That was the first time a government of this country had ever forbidden a man to grow food-and it was done by this minister. Now he comes here today and has the gall to say that income in 1974 is 90 per cent higher than it was in 1973.

speechtext: Cash receipts in Saskatchewan, in the first three quarters.

speechtext:
He says that cash receipts in Saskatchewan, for the first three quarters, are 90 per cent higher. He has the colossal gall to bring that figure to the attention of this House and leave the impression that farmers are rolling in dough. I am saying that when you take off the expenses of operation and interest charges, the farmer has barely enough to pay minimum wages. Let us compare the situation with that of 1973. In 1973, all the Saskatchewan farmer received in the full calendar year, after expenses and interest, was approximately $2,200 per family. This is the type of living condition that the minister calls rolling in dough.
Mr. Speaker, the western farmer, rightly or wrongly- but certainly of his own free will-has entered into a socialist system of marketing. He has put his fate into the hands of the Canadian Wheat Board, and quite willingly, but he expects that in return it will endeavour to get him the highest average price possible. Generally speaking, the Wheat Board has an excellent record. But having put his fate in the hands of a socialist agency over which parliament or the minister has no control, or should not have, he expects in return that this government will protect him against rises and falls in world prices.
From 1932 to 1949, farmers fought for some form of international rule of law on prices and the allocation of wheat. That was achieved in 1949 by agreement among some 50 nations, and from 1949 to 1967 wheat farmers in Australia, Canada, Argentina and the United States had the protection of an international agreement that set a floor and a ceiling on prices for a three-year period. If the price rose too high, then supply had to be guaranteed. If the price dropped to the bottom, then the demand had to be met by recipient countries on a quota basis.
This rule of law on price and allocation gave farmers a stable, though not large, income from 1949 to 1967. That held until this government, along with others, destroyed the International Wheat Agreement and replaced it with an International Grains Agreement which never took hold. All that remains is the shell of an administration framework in London, England. For the first time in a
Grain
generation, wheat farmers of the world are without an international agreement on price and allocation of supply in case of emergency.
I have sat in this House during 1972, 1973 and 1974 and have heard all about a two-price system for the little 50 million or 60 million bushels that go into domestic supply, but not one speech have I heard from the government about the billion bushels that go for export each year. Today, the grain farmers of the world who grow coarse grains and feed grains are as naked as a jay bird. The farmer in the wheat growing areas of the world, without any protection as to world price, is a streaker and does not know it. He worries about how long prices will last, because he knows that if there is a surplus of grain in the world the $5 price will drop to nothing. How will he then meet his expenses, his heavy interest rates, and so on?
The minister's talk of getting rid of the Crowsnest pass agreement has been worrying farmers. That agreement was made some 70 years ago. With 300 million bushels of grain going to export positions, the railways broke even, and now with putting a billion bushels a year into export position, the railways are making money on the Crowsnest rates. Why should the minister stir things up by saying this rate should be looked at? Two years ago he said he was going to look at the open market, and now we find ourselves in it so we must assume the minister is serious when he says he is going to do something. I did not take him seriously when he said he was going to bring us into the open market, but he did it. If he is serious about the Crowsnest base rate, we have no choice but to fight every inch of the way.
When we start talking about branch line abandonment and inland terminals, they will be tied up in our minds with the minister's new concept of western Canada. Our elevator system is 50 years out of date and our transportation system is 25 years out of date and should be replaced. We need to spend $3 billion or $4 billion on port facilities for the west coast-and goodness knows how much on the east coast. We need all these things now, and we have the technology. But all the minister does is brag about how much the farmer makes. It makes him look like one of these Montreal organized-crime types. Really, the farmer is barely earning a wage.
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say to members of the Social Credit Party. No farmer in Canada suffers more than the farmer in eastern Ontario, Quebec and the mari-times. We in the west talk about how we were just getting proper wages in 1973, but even in the good years of 1973-74 the eastern farmer was not making enough money to pay the interest on what he invested in his operation. He therefore has no income at all as far as wages are concerned. In February, 1962, a bill called the eastern feed grains assistance act was introduced in this House by this party, but was not passed because our government was defeated. There has been no indication since that successive governments have been aware that we need every eastern farmers in order to help feed a hungry world. They produce commodities that we cannot produce in western Canada because we are a desert. They can produce trees. Some hon. members will remember when a forestry act was introduced setting up a department of forestry because of the desperate need for fibre.

November 18, 1974
Grain
I do not see any sign of eastern farmers shifting into a combination of beef and tree production. All I see is a comedy of blunders in the beef industry this past year and a half. Canada does not produce enough beef to feed her own people and has to import 15 per cent of her needs. We draw on the protein supplies of the world for 15 per cent of our needs. By unilaterally removing our tariff in 1973 and encouraging farmers to flood our market with a few thousand head of cattle, the government destroyed the price base and has played ping-pong with beef ever since.
Madam Speaker, I think this legislation, regardless of its apparent function-and it is there, obviously, to carry out a firm moral principle-is sound legislation. The $15,000 ceiling now is the same as the $6,000 ceiling in earlier days. The purpose of the legislation is fundamentally sound, that is, to keep the farmer from going too deeply into the open market system at the present time. In the main, I think the legislation should be supported.
I conclude with this fundamental position. I ask the minister to take his mind off the Crowsnest rates for a while and to re-establish the International Wheat Agreement so that farmers who produce grain will be governed by a stable rule of law which will take care of prices and allocation of supplies for the next 10 or 15 years. If he does that, he can make his next four years in parliament worth while.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-10 amends the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, an act that has been well accepted across the prairies and was brought in by the government headed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), as previously stated. It was introduced during the 1957-58 crop year. Back in those days the advance was paid at the rate of 50 cents per bushel for wheat, 20 cents per bushel for oats and 35 cents per bushel for barley, the maximum of $3,000 being paid to any one producer.
The amendment before the House shows the dramatic increase in operating expenses for western grain agriculture. The act was amended in 1968 and payments were increased to $1 per bushel for wheat, 40 cents per bushel for oats and 70 cents per bushel for barley. The maximum for any producer was increased to $6,000. These cash advances are based on wheat, oats and barley harvested and in storage in the farmer's bins. The farmer, of course, must await quota levels which will allow him to deliver his grain to the Wheat Board and he pledges to deliver the committed grain as the quotas open. As has been said, the cash advance is not a hand-out by the federal government; it is actually the farmer's own money, paid to him while he is awaiting delivery quotas. If the producer is in default, appropriate action is taken even up to prosecution.
The present legislation places an additional administrative burden on the Canadian Wheat Board and country grain elevators. In 1972-73, the number of accounts in default totalled 3,538. Altogether, 1,468 accounts were taken to the Federal Court of Canada. Overdue accounts tend to create bad feeling between the grain buyer and the grain producer. Over the years, more than $1 billion has been taken by the producers in cash advances and the

repayment record has been very good, only a small fraction-less than 1 per cent of accounts owing-remaining unpaid. This year, already $28 million in cash advances has been taken out by producers, clearly establishing the need for this legislation.
As I said previously, the Canadian Wheat Board has been assigned the responsibility of administering this act which has been in existence now for about 17 years. The effects of grain companies being agents of the Wheat Board have filtered down to the country grain buyer. Thus we see the government continually sloughing off its responsibilities to grain companies. They are forced to act as agents of the government, with all the political implications involved. When the producer gets a cash advance, he goes straight to the bank or credit union with it. That is where the transaction should take place. Initially the forms might be held by the country elevator and, if necessary, signed by the grain buyer or a commissioner for oaths, as happens at present. Nevertheless, the entire administration of cash advances is properly the business of our banking system which should be responsible for the collection of this money.
We have piled far too much work on our country elevator operators. I have talked to these people, and it is apparent that unless the system is changed we shall experience real difficulty in recruiting men to fulfil this function. Only in the last two years have country grain buyers in Saskatchewan been relieved of the responsibility of collecting overdue municipal taxes. That was an unjust responsibility. The federal government is still piling responsibilities on these companies and involving them in this greatly expanded cash advance legislation.
The fact that advances are to increase to $15,000 per individual, $30,000 for two people and $45,000 for three, shows the extent to which farm production costs have escalated. Although $15,000 may sound like a lot of money, it represents two truckloads of flax or, in other words, 1,500 bushels of flax or one hopper car of wheat. The producer is to pay full income tax on the advance in the year in which it is taken out. He may exercise the other option, of course, and take out a bank loan; in that case he will pay the tax in the year in which it is repaid. I should think the government could give the producer a break by deferring payment: it could require him to pay tax in the year he repays his cash advance.
I support this legislation, with two reservations. This is just one more law which tends to isolate the producer from the marketplace. For instance, during the west coast grain tie-up producers were not affected directly because so many laws come between them and their actual pay cheque. This is another such law. Finally, I ask the minister not to overload grain buyers with paper work. Let him be careful to avoid that in this and in future legislation.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE DEDUCTIONS FOR VOLUNTEER SERVICES PROVIDED FOR CHARITABLE ORGANIZATIONS AND GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to provide for deductions for volunteer services provided by a taxpayer on behalf of either a charitable organization or a federal, provincial or municipal agency.

He said: Madam Speaker, volunteer workers comprise one of the main groups in this country who keep certain activities alive in our communities. I know the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has great concern in this respect. During the last election campaign he mentioned across the country that he was going to set up a committee or a council on voluntarism. Two weeks ago the minister was speaking before the advisory council on voluntarism, and I should like to read into the record a report by the Canadian Press calling attention to some of his statements:
The advisory council on voluntarism should suggest ways in which the federal government and voluntary organizations can co-operate to improve the quality of life in Canada, Secretary of State Hugh Faulkner said Sunday.
Faulkner, speaking at a conference of national voluntary organizations, announced the appointment of 15 members to the council.
Establishment of the council, which has a two-year mandate, was announced during the election campaign in June.
The minister suggested that the problems of recruiting members and financing volunteer organizations be studied by the advisory council.
He said: "There is a great need for more collaboration between the federal government, the voluntary organizations, the foundations, and the corporations to avoid duplication and to encourage a more rational use of limited resources. The council's advice in this area would be particularly welcome."
The minister also suggested that further study be made into the government policy of subsidizing organizations which oppose its policies. He added: "I believe it is a sign of healthy and vital democracy if governments feel able to subsidize constructive dissent".
He mentioned as examples of this policy grants to women's groups and native organizations which often criticize government.
The possibility of subsidizing intervention by voluntary organizations before regulatory bodies such as the National Energy Board or the Canadian Transport Commission should also be studied by the council, he said.
The conference has gathered for the first time leaders of about 60 national voluntary groups such as the Red Cross, the Boy Scouts of Canada and La Federation des Femmes Canadiennes Francises to discuss matters of mutual concern.
Volunteers in this country are doing a great job: I do not think anybody would deny that. We have cases of people
Income Tax Act
throughout this country driving their cars once a week from, for example, my constituency which is 20 miles from a major hospital where a great deal of work is done. People use their cars to drive others who cannot walk and are in wheelchairs to hospitals every morning. This costs them a great deal of money for which they are receiving no compensation whatsoever. We have people coaching soccer teams, football teams and hockey teams. They go to great expense. I know in my own case, as a member of parliament often away from home during the week, the coach of my three sons soccer teams has to come to my house to pick up my children because there isn't a bus service in the area, this involves his driving an extra 20 miles every time they play soccer, which is six time a week for the three of them.
These are expenses being met out of people's pockets, sometimes people who cannot really afford it. Yet they look around and they see OFY grants and LIP grants that are not always meeting the needs of various areas. I do not want to be too critical in this area because many of us have set up advisory groups for these programs and they are much improved over what they were a couple of years ago. But I still think there is a bad taste left in many people's mouths over some of the grants that have been handed out in the past.
These volunteers are seeing a society that seems to be spending more money on welfare than they think should be spent. They are seeing waste by government. I think a good case of waste is the government's funding of this volunteer organization to the tune of $10,000. Is this the type of money we want the government to be spending? The volunteer organization which the government is supporting and setting up may come up with many useful ideas; but one of its main points, we hear from the minister, is that it is to recommend to various volunteer organizations just where they should go in government to obtain money. I thought Information Canada was set up for that purpose. Why do we need another bureaucracy to tell people where they should go to get funds from government? Information Canada was set up for that purpose and it should be used for that purpose, as should the minister's offices.
I do not intend to speak very long on this subject because I think it is straightforward. It is explained in the motion. We are asking the government to consider the feasibility of allowing volunteer workers to get a tax deduction for the amount of money they spend out of their own pockets on volunteer work. This is being done in many countries. I do not think it is too much to ask the government to consider this suggestion. I know, in a motion of this type and in a major financial area such as this, the government will want time to study the proposal and determine whether it is feasible. I am not an economic specialist and I do not know whether it is totally feasible, but I think at least we should bring the subject before a committee so it can be discussed. That is where full discussion should take place, in committees of the House and not in organizations outside the House of Commons.
I have spoken to many volunteer organizations that are having a hard time getting volunteers to work for them. They are getting a throwback from these people who are saying, "I would love very much to take Mr. Jones down to

Let us not stand here for an hour and talk about this, Madam Speaker: let us put it into a committee and discuss it. I think we can discuss it in committee on a non-partisan basis because I do not think it is a partisan subject. I hope the government will not take up the 47 minutes that are left.
